false_positives.candidate:
Changing live span keys from sets to sorted sets has no migration path

This now executes ZADD against `span-buf:s:*` keys, while deployed versions created these keys as Redis sets. During a rolling deployment, any active buffered trace with a pre-existing set will make ZADD fail with WRONGTYPE (and later ZSCAN/ZCARD and the Lua script will fail similarly). A single such key can fail the pipeline/batch and prevent span processing until the old key expires, losing or delaying spans. Use a versioned key namespace or explicitly migrate/handle legacy set keys before issuing sorted-set commands.

Lua eviction bypasses the configurable segment-size limit

The script unconditionally retains only 1,000 members, while `SpansBuffer.max_segment_spans` remains a constructor option and was previously enforced by `_load_segment_data`. Configurations below 1,000 are no longer honored (oversized segments are emitted rather than rejected), and configurations above 1,000 silently lose spans. The configured limit needs to be passed to the script and used for eviction, or the obsolete option and its contract need to be removed consistently.

Reducing redirect traversal depth can split valid deep traces

Redirect resolution was reduced from 10,000 links to 1,000. For a trace whose parent chain exceeds 1,000 spans and arrives out of order, the loop stops before reaching the existing segment root, stores the span under an intermediate key, and produces separate/incomplete segments. The prior code explicitly documented the depth limit as the condition under which trees can fail to merge; lowering it is a functional regression unless ingestion guarantees a maximum depth of 1,000.

They then serialize on this write lock, but every waiter unconditionally rereads and reparses the manifest instead of using the value populated by the first request. A burst of startup requests therefore causes O(n) sequential filesystem reads/parses and delays each request. After acquiring the write lock, check `cfg.Env != setting.Dev && entryPointAssetsCache != nil` again and return the cached value before performing I/O.

false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes inherit the request cancellation context

The goroutine derives its 10-second context from the original request context. HTTP/API-server request contexts are normally canceled as soon as the handler returns, which happens immediately after this goroutine is started, so the legacy Create will usually receive an already-canceled context rather than up to 10 seconds to complete. The same pattern is used by Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection (lines 110, 135, and 163), making the asynchronous replication unreliable or effectively skipped for normal completed requests. Detach cancellation (while preserving required context values/logging) before applying the timeout.

Independent replication goroutines can apply mutations out of order

Each successful write starts an independent goroutine with no per-resource ordering or serialization. For example, a successful unified Create followed immediately by Delete can run the legacy Delete first and the legacy Create second, leaving an object in legacy that no longer exists in unified storage. Consecutive updates can similarly overwrite newer legacy state with an older update. Since legacy APIs remain available as the stated safety measure, this produces persistent cross-store divergence; replication needs an ordered queue/keyed serialization or another ordering mechanism.

Legacy Update re-executes the original UpdatedObjectInfo instead of replaying the unified result

After Storage.Update has already evaluated objInfo against the unified object, the asynchronous legacy update receives the original objInfo and evaluates it again against legacy state. This regresses the prior implementation, which evaluated the update once and wrapped the resulting object for each store. UpdatedObjectInfo can represent a PATCH/apply operation and can depend on the old object, resource version, managed fields, or request-specific state; evaluating it again can yield a different object or fail due to the legacy object's version. As a result, successful unified updates may not be mirrored correctly to legacy. Capture and replay the object produced by the unified update (using an appropriate wrapper) rather than reusing objInfo.

Create storage failures are attributed to legacy metrics

When Storage.Create fails, the code calls `recordLegacyDuration` rather than `recordStorageDuration`. The analogous Update error path at line 129 has the same issue. Storage write failures in mode 3 will therefore be missing from storage error metrics and falsely inflate legacy errors, obscuring which backend failed.

Mode 3 tests do not verify asynchronous legacy replication

The tests return immediately after the unified operation and never wait for or assert the background legacy call. Moreover, both `legacyStoreMock` and `storageMock` share one testify Mock and define identical method expectations, so an expectation configured as a storage call can also satisfy the legacy call; there is no `AssertExpectations` call to establish that either occurred. Consequently these tests would pass if replication never runs (including when the caller context is canceled), and they do not detect the ordering or Update replay regressions. Use distinct backend mocks and synchronization (for example a channel/WaitGroup) to assert the legacy call and its arguments.

In the new ruler-free Grafana list, a rule can be reported as pausable from its Prometheus representation while no Pause/Resume menu item is rendered, removing pause control from the list.

false_positives.candidate:
Unsubscribe state is changed through a cross-site GET request

The new `unsubscribe` action changes `TopicUser.notification_level` on a GET route, and the action is explicitly excluded from the XHR check. GET requests are not protected by Rails CSRF tokens, so any third-party page can cause a logged-in visitor's browser to request `/t/<slug>/<id>/unsubscribe` and silently alter that visitor's topic notification state. This should be a CSRF-protected non-GET action (with the email link leading to a confirmation page), or use a purpose-specific signed unsubscribe token.

Direct TopicUser save does not record this as a user-selected notification level

The action updates and saves the `TopicUser` record directly instead of using `TopicUser.change`, which is the normal notification-level update path. Consequently it leaves `notifications_reason_id` and `notifications_changed_at` unchanged. In particular, a topic-user row whose reason is still nil can subsequently satisfy `TopicUser.auto_track`'s `notifications_reason_id: nil` check and be automatically changed back to tracking, undoing a user's mute/unsubscribe choice. Use `TopicUser.change(current_user, topic_id, notification_level: ...)` so the change is marked with the `user_changed` reason and published consistently.

Typo in property name: 'stopNotificiationsText' should be 'stopNotificationsText' (missing 'n' in 'Notifications')

true_positives.golden_comment: logic: macOS-specific sed syntax with empty string after -i flag will fail on Linux systems
true_positives.matched_candidate:
The env-file update command fails on GNU/Linux sed

`sed -i '' -E ...` uses BSD/macOS `sed` syntax. On GNU sed, which is used by typical Linux development and CI environments, the separated empty argument is treated as an input filename (or otherwise causes an error), so an existing `GOOGLE_WEBHOOK_URL` is not updated. Use a portable temporary-file replacement or select the `sed -i` form based on the platform.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments say that `sed -i ''` is BSD/macOS-only syntax and breaks on GNU/Linux sed. They describe the same issue.

false_positives.candidate:
Deleting cache does not invalidate the displayed calendar cache status

The delete-cache mutation only invokes the optional onSuccess callback. Unlike the disconnect mutation, it never invalidates `viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars`. In this wrapper `onChanged` is optional, so after a successful deletion the active query can retain its previous `cacheUpdatedAt` indefinitely (window-focus refetch is disabled), continuing to show cache status and the delete action for data that no longer exists. Invalidate or refetch `viewer.calendars.connectedCalendars` when the deletion settles.

The cron development command relies on an undeclared, unpinned tsx executable

`tsx` is not declared in this workspace's dependencies or devDependencies, so `npx tsx` must resolve/download whatever current registry version is available when the command is run (and can fail in offline/CI or non-interactive environments). This makes `yarn dev:cron` non-reproducible and can execute an unexpected version. Add a pinned `tsx` dependency and invoke its workspace binary (or use the existing declared runner).

false_negatives.golden_comment: The updateManyByCredentialId call uses an empty data object, which prevents Prisma's @updatedAt decorator from updating the updatedAt timestamp. This results in inaccurate cache status tracking, as the timestamp isn't updated when the cache is refreshed. To fix this, explicitly set the updatedAt field.

Throwing a generic Error for authentication failures results in a 500 response in tRPC. Instead, it should return a structured TRPCError with an appropriate code, such as FORBIDDEN, to accurately reflect the error type.
Date is formatted with hardcoded 'en-US' locale instead of using the user's locale from useLocale, which can lead to incorrect date representation for users in different locales.

true_positives.golden_comment: Incorrect end time calculation using slotStartTime instead of slotEndTime
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Fixed-host working-hours validation ignores the event duration

`end` is calculated from `slotStartTime` exactly as `start` is, so the condition only verifies that the slot starts before `workingHour.endTime`; it never verifies that the event ends before it. For round-robin events with a fixed host, a slot generated from a loose host's availability can therefore be retained even though the fixed host's shift ends partway through the event (for example, a 60-minute event starting at 09:30 with the fixed host available only until 10:00). The end value must include `eventLength` and be checked against the fixed host's availability.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments point to the same bug: the end time is computed from slotStartTime, so it equals the start, when it should use the slot end (start plus event length). The golden comment says to use slotEndTime and the candidate says to include eventLength, which amount to the same fix.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Zero-length date overrides are never recognized as such

The code compares two newly-created Dayjs objects with `===`, which compares object identity and is always false even when `date.start` and `date.end` represent the same instant. Consequently, the special handling for a zero-length/full-day override never executes. Such an override can leave a slot at its boundary available instead of marking the host unavailable, allowing a booking during an intended day off. Compare the timestamps (for example with `isSame`) instead.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments point to the same bug: comparing dayjs objects with === checks reference identity, so it is always false. Both also recommend isSame as the fix.

false_positives.candidate:
Multiple override windows on one day are treated as an intersection

The `find` callback returns `true` when a slot is outside any individual override window, and the outer code immediately rejects the slot. If a host has two availability override ranges on the same date, a slot inside the first range is necessarily outside the second range and is rejected. This makes all slots unavailable whenever date overrides contain multiple separate windows, rather than accepting slots covered by at least one window. The logic should first collect the overrides for the date and accept a slot if it fits within any applicable override range.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 reads a possibly stale value and can lose increments under concurrency; consider an atomic increment via Prisma (increment: 1) to avoid race conditions (also applies to the similar update in the catch block).
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Retry counts can be lost when cron executions overlap

The retry value is read in `findMany` and then written back as `reminder.retryCount + 1`. If two authorized cron invocations process the same unscheduled reminder concurrently, both can read (for example) 0 and both write 1 after failures. The row will then receive an extra retry despite two failed scheduling attempts, so the intended two-attempt limit is not enforced (and concurrent executions can continue submitting duplicate provider requests). Use an atomic database increment and/or atomically claim the reminder before scheduling; the catch-path update at line 195 has the same lost-update issue.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments flag the same problem. Reading retryCount and writing reminder.retryCount + 1 can lose increments when updates run concurrently. Both suggest an atomic increment instead, and both say the catch-block update has the same flaw.

true_positives.golden_comment: The deletion logic in scheduleSMSReminders.ts incorrectly deletes non-SMS workflow reminders (e.g., Email, WhatsApp) that have retryCount > 1. This occurs because the retryCount condition within the OR clause for deletion lacks a method: WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, causing it to apply to all reminder types instead of only SMS reminders, which is the intended scope of this function.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Retry cleanup is not restricted to SMS reminders

The new `retryCount > 1` branch is an OR condition without a `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` constraint. Consequently, any non-SMS `WorkflowReminder` (for example, email or WhatsApp) whose retryCount exceeds one will be permanently deleted by this SMS cron endpoint, even though this job neither schedules nor owns those reminder types. Keep the retry threshold inside an SMS-scoped condition so this destructive cleanup cannot remove unrelated workflow reminder records.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug. The retryCount > 1 OR branch lacks an SMS method filter, so the SMS cron deletes non-SMS reminders such as Email and WhatsApp.

false_positives.candidate:
Reminders with no sendable message or recipient never consume retries

RetryCount is incremented only after `scheduleSMS` returns false or throws. When `message` is empty/null or `sendTo` is absent, the condition at this line is skipped entirely, leaving the reminder `scheduled: false` and `retryCount` unchanged. The cron will select and reprocess that permanently unsendable reminder on every run until its scheduled date, which preserves the retry loop this change is intended to stop. Mark these cases as failed attempts (or delete/cancel them explicitly) so they are bounded by the same retry policy.

The public findMany API was removed without a replacement query API

This change deletes `findMany`, which previously applied authorization and filter conditions and returned records from `bookingTimeStatusDenormalized`. `getBaseConditions` only returns a SQL fragment; it does not accept or apply the caller's `findMany` arguments, perform the query, or provide an equivalent typed result API. Existing consumers of the exported `InsightsBookingService` that call `findMany` will fail to compile/runtime, and consumers migrated only to this method must reimplement query construction and risk omitting authorization conditions. Preserve `findMany` or introduce an equivalent supported raw-query method and migrate all callers atomically.

Team and organization raw authorization predicates are never executed against the database

The team and org tests only compare `Prisma.Sql` objects constructed by the service with `Prisma.Sql` objects constructed in the expectation. They do not execute the predicates. The sole `$queryRaw` test at lines 481-484 uses user scope, which has neither the `ANY(${...})` array bindings nor the OR branches used by team/org authorization. Consequently, PostgreSQL serialization/type errors for array parameters, SQL precedence issues, or predicates that return unauthorized/missing bookings in the team and org scopes can pass this suite. Add database-backed tests for both scopes, including matching and non-matching team and member bookings.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In getBaseConditions(), the else if (filterConditions) and final else branches are unreachable. This is because getAuthorizationConditions() always returns a non-null Prisma.Sql object, making authConditions always truthy, which means only the first two if/else if conditions are ever evaluated.

Fetching userIdsFromOrg only when teamsFromOrg.length > 0 can exclude org-level members for orgs without child teams; consider deriving from teamIds (which includes orgId) or removing the guard so org-only orgs still include member user bookings.

true_positives.matched_candidate:

Both computed property names evaluate to the same string (`"[object Object]"`), with the latter overwriting the former; they do not define a numeric-key catch-all. Moreover, `z.object` strips unknown keys by default. When credential syncing is enabled, a response such as `{ access_token, expiry_date }` is therefore parsed down to just `access_token` (plus the fabricated refresh token below). Callers then store an undefined/invalid expiry, causing tokens to be considered expired on every request; Zoom can persist `NaN` for `expiry_date`.

The golden comment says this is invalid Zod syntax that throws at runtime. The candidate says the keys collapse to "[object Object]" and unknown keys get stripped, so expiry data is lost. The predicted consequences differ, but the root issue is the same misuse of computed keys.

true_positives.golden_comment: When APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are set, the refreshFunction helper returns the fetch Response, but several callers (for example GoogleCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting res.data, and HubspotCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting a HubspotToken) assume it returns the integration-specific token object. The sync branch returns the native `fetch` `Response`, while several existing callers expect their provider/axios response object directly. For example, HubSpot reads `expiresIn` and `accessToken` from the returned value, and the Zoho Bigin/CRM services read `tokenInfo.data`; those properties do not exist on a Fetch `Response`. Enabling `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` therefore makes refreshes for these integrations fail or save undefined token fields. The helper needs a normalized result contract (or all callers must explicitly parse the response consistently).
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same problem: in sync mode, refreshFunction returns a fetch Response, while callers such as HubSpot expect provider token objects. That mismatch causes runtime failures. The candidate cites slightly different examples (Zoho instead of Google), but the underlying issue is identical.

Enabling `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` therefore makes refreshes for these integrations fail or save undefined token fields. Both call for a consistent return shape. The golden comment cites a different specific caller, but the underlying issue is identical.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `refreshOAuthTokens` function is passed `credentialId` instead of `userId`, which breaks the credential sync functionality by causing incorrect user lookups. This issue can lead to failures in syncing user credentials, impacting user experience.

`refreshOAuthTokens` expects its third argument to be a user ID and serializes it as `calcomUserId`, but this call passes `credentialId` rather than `credential.userId`. false_positives.candidate:
Salesforce service references Prisma without importing it

`prisma.credential.update` is called here, but this file has no `prisma` import. Type checking/building the app-store package will fail with `Cannot find name 'prisma'`, blocking the application build.

Zoom refresh requests use a different app slug than the installed app

The outbound sync payload identifies this integration as `zoomvideo`, whereas the Zoom app/credential is consistently identified as `zoom` (for example, the OAuth callback creates `appId: "zoom"`). A source application that routes refreshes by app slug will not recognize this request, so Zoom credential sync cannot refresh successfully.

The shared refresh helper documents that a sync endpoint returns only an access token and expiry, but Webex bypasses the relaxed parser and validates the response with `webexRefreshedTokenSchema`, which requires `scope`, `token_type`, `refresh_token`, and `refresh_token_expires_in`. Consequently, a conforming sync endpoint response is always rejected and Webex refresh fails whenever syncing is enabled.

This newly added Salesforce refresh always posts directly to Salesforce and never calls `refreshOAuthTokens` or checks `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT`. Thus Salesforce is one of the modified integrations for which enabling credential syncing has no effect, contrary to the feature's source-of-truth behavior.

Credential create/update is not atomic and can create duplicate credentials

The handler performs `findFirst` and then separately creates a credential if none was found. Concurrent webhook deliveries for the same user and app can both observe no row and both create one. Since the code explicitly cannot use an upsert and there is no shown uniqueness constraint, duplicate credentials can remain; downstream integrations commonly use `findFirst`, making the selected credential nondeterministic. Use a transaction with an appropriate unique constraint/upsert or otherwise serialize this operation.

This invalidates the token, breaking subsequent token refreshes and causing authentication failures.

The Salesforce integration checks `response.statusText` instead of `response.ok` when handling OAuth token refresh responses. This can lead to unreliable behavior, as a successful response may not be correctly identified, resulting in the use of stale credentials and potential authentication failures.

The `appCredentialWebhookRequestBodySchema.parse` function can throw on invalid payloads, resulting in 500 Internal Server Errors instead of the expected 400 Bad Request responses. This can lead to confusion for clients and hinder proper error handling.

false_positives.candidate:
Cancellations can wait until after the reminder has been sent

Cancelled email reminders are only submitted to SendGrid when this 15-minute cron next runs and the reminder is within the next hour. For example, if a reminder is due in five minutes and the booking is cancelled immediately after a cron run, no cancellation request is made for up to 15 minutes, so SendGrid can deliver the reminder at its scheduled time. This leaves the primary cancelled-booking case unfixed for reminders cancelled shortly before they are due; cancellation needs to be performed promptly enough to beat the send time (or the scheduling job needs to run with a sufficiently tight guarantee).

Expired cancelled reminders are deleted without cancelling their SendGrid send

The expired-reminder cleanup runs before the new cancellation loop and deletes every email reminder whose scheduledDate is at or before now, including rows marked cancelled. If the cron is late or SendGrid has not yet processed a send scheduled for that timestamp, the local record is removed and the later cancellation pass can no longer submit the required SendGrid cancellation. The scheduled email can consequently still be delivered, and there is no remaining row to retry cancellation. Cancelled reminders should be handled/cancelled before generic expiry cleanup, and failed cancellations should remain retryable.

false_negatives.golden_comment: Asynchronous functions deleteScheduledEmailReminder and deleteScheduledSMSReminder are called without await inside forEach loops. This occurs during booking rescheduling/cancellation, and workflow/workflow step deletion/updates. Consequently, scheduled workflow reminders may not be reliably cancelled, potentially leaving them active.

When immediateDelete is true, the deleteScheduledEmailReminder function cancels the SendGrid email but fails to delete the corresponding WorkflowReminder record from the database. This creates orphaned database entries and is inconsistent with the immediateDelete: false path, which marks the record as cancelled. The SendGrid DELETE API call is also omitted in this path.

The 'cancelled' field is nullable, which can lead to existing records having null values instead of a default of false. This can cause incorrect behavior in the application when checking the cancellation status of reminders.

true_positives.golden_comment: The logic for checking team admin/owner permissions is incorrect. This condition uses AND (&&) which requires both isTeamAdmin AND isTeamOwner to be true, but it should use OR (||) since a user needs to be either an admin OR an owner to have permission.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Team admins and owners are incorrectly denied permission to add guests

The team permission check combines `isTeamAdmin` and `isTeamOwner` with `&&`. A membership normally has one of these roles, so a team admin who is not the booking's assigned organizer (and an owner if the helpers are role-specific) fails this check even though the UI explicitly exposes this action to `isUserTeamAdminOrOwner`. Use `||` (or the project’s established combined-role authorization helper) so either privileged team role is accepted.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments point to the same bug: the isTeamAdmin and isTeamOwner checks are joined with && when they should use ||. Because of this, team admins and owners are wrongly denied permission.

true_positives.golden_comment: The sendAddGuestsEmails function in email-manager.ts passes the full calendarEvent.attendees array when determining which attendees receive AttendeeScheduledEmail vs AttendeeAddGuestsEmail, but checks if newGuests.includes(attendee.email) where newGuests is the input guests array.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Existing addresses in a mixed request receive a new-booking email

The email sender is passed the original `guests` array rather than `uniqueGuests`. If a request contains one already-attending email plus one genuinely new email, `sendAddGuestsEmails` classifies the existing attendee as a newly added guest and sends it `AttendeeScheduledEmail` (a booking confirmation) even though no attendee was added for that address. Pass the filtered list of actually-created emails to ensure only new invitees receive the scheduled email.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug. sendAddGuestsEmails checks newGuests.includes(attendee.email) against the raw input guests array instead of the deduplicated list, so attendees who already exist can be misclassified and sent AttendeeScheduledEmail.

true_positives.golden_comment: uniqueGuests filters out existing attendees and blacklisted emails but does not deduplicate duplicates within the input; createMany can insert duplicate attendee rows if the client submits repeated emails.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
The API permits duplicate guest emails in a single request

`uniqueGuests` only filters out attendees that existed before this mutation; it never deduplicates `guests` itself. Although the dialog validates duplicates, callers can invoke the tRPC endpoint directly because the server schema has no uniqueness refinement. A request such as `["guest@example.com", "guest@example.com"]` therefore attempts to create duplicate attendee records (or fails the entire operation if a database uniqueness constraint exists), and can produce duplicate calendar/email effects. Deduplicate and normalize the input server-side, or reject duplicate input before `createMany`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments describe the same bug: uniqueGuests filters out existing attendees but never deduplicates repeated emails within the input itself, so createMany can insert duplicate attendee rows.

false_positives.candidate:
Attendee-initiated updates use the attendee's calendar credentials instead of the organizer's

The handler explicitly authorizes any existing attendee at line 52, but obtains credentials from `ctx.user` here. For an attendee adding a guest, these are the attendee's integrations, not the booking organizer's destination-calendar credentials. `updateCalendarAttendees` will consequently be unable to update the organizer's calendar (or may target an inappropriate connected calendar), after the attendee rows have already been inserted. Resolve credentials for the booking owner/calendar connection when updating the booking's calendar.

A calendar-update failure leaves permanently inconsistent booking state

The new attendees are committed to the database at lines 92-106 before the external calendar update is attempted here. If `updateCalendarAttendees` throws, the mutation returns an error but the database still contains the guests; retrying then filters those emails as already present and rejects the request, so the caller cannot repair the missing calendar invitation/update through this feature. Add compensation/retry handling or structure the operation so failed external synchronization is recorded and can be retried rather than treating the database write as a completed update.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The addGuests.handler.ts blacklist check uses blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest) after lowercasing the blacklist but not the input guest emails, allowing attackers to bypass BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS restrictions by submitting emails with uppercase characters.
Starting with an array containing an empty string may cause validation issues. Consider starting with an empty array [] and handling the empty state in the MultiEmail component instead.

The `sendAddGuestsEmails` function does not check the `disableStandardEmails` flags in the `EventType` metadata, which may result in sending emails to hosts/attendees even when standard emails are disabled for the event type.

true_positives.golden_comment: Because backupCodes are decrypted and mutated in memory before being written back, two concurrent login requests using the same backupCode could both pass this check and update, so a single backup code may effectively be accepted more than once if used concurrently, weakening the intended one-time-use semantics.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Consume backup codes atomically

The backup code is read and validated from the initially fetched user record, then a separate unconditional update writes the modified array. Two credential requests using the same code can both read the unconsumed value before either update executes, both pass validation, and both receive sessions. This violates the stated exactly-once property and can let an attacker who races a legitimate user reuse a stolen code. Consume the code through a transaction/row lock or a conditional update that verifies the stored value has not changed, and reject the request when that update affects no rows.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same race condition: concurrent login requests with the same backup code each pass validation before the in-memory modified array is written back, so a one-time code can be used more than once.

false_positives.candidate:
Backup codes cannot be used in the external-provider 2FA flow

The new backup-code branch is unreachable for users entering the `/auth/login?totp=...` flow used after Google/SAML authentication. Before this branch, line 113 rejects every non-CAL identity provider when `credentials.totpCode` is absent; a backup-code submission intentionally has no TOTP code. The login UI also renders `ExternalTotpFooter` for this flow, which provides no "Lost access" option. Consequently, users with external-provider accounts protected by 2FA cannot use their backup codes to recover access.

The backup-code authentication and one-time-use behavior is untested

The added test coverage only verifies that the backup-code screen can copy/download data. It never submits a backup code through login or the disable-2FA recovery flow, and never verifies that a successfully used code is rejected on a subsequent attempt. These are the primary new authentication and security semantics, so regressions such as codes not being passed to NextAuth or not being consumed would pass the current suite.

Error message mentions 'backup code login' but this is a disable endpoint, not login

Backup code validation is case-sensitive due to the use of indexOf(). This causes validation to fail if a user enters uppercase hex characters, as backup codes should be case-insensitive for a better user experience.

Object URL for backup codes is not revoked on component unmount, leading to a potential memory leak. This can cause increased memory usage over time, especially if the component is mounted and unmounted frequently.

false_positives.candidate:
Google Meet fallback dereferences an absent destination calendar

`mainHostDestinationCalendar` is `undefined` when an event has no destination calendar, which is a supported case handled later by the fallback calendar logic. For a Google Meet event, the condition evaluates `mainHostDestinationCalendar.integration` unconditionally and throws instead of falling back to Cal Video. This breaks booking creation for Google Meet events without a selected destination calendar.

Office 365 always creates collective events in the first host calendar

Each collective destination is processed with its own credential by `EventManager`, but this service ignores the credential being used and always selects `event.destinationCalendar[0]`. Consequently, when a collective booking has multiple Office 365 hosts, later hosts either attempt to create the event in the first host's calendar using their own token (often failing authorization) or create duplicates there; their configured destination calendars are never used.

Lark creation ignores destinations after the first collective host

The multi-destination creation loop constructs a Lark service for each destination credential, but `createEvent` always takes the first entry in `event.destinationCalendar`. Thus all Lark host creations target the first host's calendar rather than the destination associated with the credential currently being processed, so collective Lark hosts do not receive their calendar events.

CalDAV creation cannot target each collective destination

CalDAV event creation filters calendars using only `event.destinationCalendar[0]`. `EventManager` invokes this service once per destination/credential, but the selected destination external ID is not passed into the service, so every invocation targets the first host's calendar. Collective events with multiple CalDAV destinations will therefore be duplicated in or fail against the first destination and omitted from the other hosts' calendars.

Recurring collective cancellation deletes only the first calendar reference under every credential

For each calendar reference, the recurring-cancellation branch iterates every calendar credential but obtains each recurring booking's reference with `.find(...)`, which always selects only the first calendar reference. With the new multiple-host references, it repeatedly attempts to delete that first event through all credentials and never selects the corresponding references for the other host calendars. Cancelling all remaining instances of a collective recurring booking consequently leaves events on other hosts' calendars (and can issue deletes against unrelated calendars).

The optional chaining on mainHostDestinationCalendar?.integration is redundant since you already check mainHostDestinationCalendar in the ternary condition.

Logic error: when externalCalendarId is provided, you're searching for a calendar where externalId === externalCalendarId, but this will always fail since you're looking for a calendar that matches itself. Should likely find by credentialId or use different logic.

Logic inversion in organization creation: The slug property is now conditionally set when IS_TEAM_BILLING_ENABLED is true, instead of when it's false as originally intended. Reschedule mutation does not await dynamic calendar deletion

This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.

Calendar/video deletion promises are detached during rescheduling

Because `getCalendar` now always awaits a dynamic-import promise before `deleteEvent` is invoked, this function proceeds to send the reschedule email and returns without waiting for deletion to start or finish. Rejections from either the import or the provider deletion also bypass the surrounding `try/catch` and can become unhandled rejections. Use `await Promise.all(bookingRefsFiltered.map(async ...))` (or an awaited `for...of`) so cancellation is completed and failures are handled before the operation finishes.

Validate the flusher process count as a positive integer

`--flusher-processes` accepts zero and negative values. Zero is silently converted to the number of assigned shards by `max_processes or len(...)`, violating the documented maximum, while a negative value reaches `range(self.num_processes)` with a negative count and then raises `KeyError` when shard assignment indexes a nonexistent process entry. A bad deployment/config value can therefore either unexpectedly spawn one worker per shard or prevent the span consumer from starting. Use a Click integer range with a minimum of 1 (and defensively validate the constructor argument).

The new flusher-process test never exercises multiprocessing

Supplying `produce_to_pipe=messages.append` intentionally makes `SpanFlusher` create `threading.Thread` workers rather than spawned processes. This test only verifies the in-memory shard-to-worker mapping; it cannot catch failures in the production path such as spawning, pickling `SpansBuffer`/synchronization values, Sentry initialization, or process lifecycle behavior. Add an integration-style test that uses the normal producer setup (mocking Kafka as needed) and verifies multiple spawned workers can flush assigned shards.

Uses Queue shutdown APIs unavailable on supported Python versions

`queue.Queue.shutdown()` and `queue.ShutDown` were introduced in Python 3.13. Each work queue is created with the default unbounded `queue.Queue()`, so `submit()` at line 212 never blocks when a worker or a particular queue is slow. The Kafka consumer can therefore continue accepting messages indefinitely while work accumulates in memory, eventually causing an OOM rather than applying the documented “natural backpressure when queues fill up.” Configure a bounded queue size and ensure the processing strategy/poll loop handles a full queue safely.

Graceful shutdown abandons queued work instead of draining it

A worker that finishes its current item exits on the next loop condition even when its queue still contains items, so queued offsets remain outstanding and work is not processed. `join()` then invokes this shutdown path as well, despite its expected role of waiting for in-flight work. This causes processed-but-uncommitted or partially processed results to be replayed after a normal consumer shutdown, risking duplicate side effects; drain queues before stopping workers and perform a final commit of completed offsets.

Processing failures are acknowledged and committed

The worker catches every exception from `result_processor` but unconditionally calls `complete_offset` in `finally`. The commit loop will then advance the Kafka offset past a failed result, permanently dropping it instead of retrying or routing it through the consumer's failure handling. This also contradicts the strategy's stated guarantee that offsets are committed only after successful processing. false_positives.candidate:
Async legacy writes inherit the request cancellation context

The goroutine derives its 10-second context from the original request context. HTTP/API-server request contexts are normally canceled as soon as the handler returns, which happens immediately after this goroutine is started, so the legacy Create will usually receive an already-canceled context rather than up to 10 seconds to complete. The same pattern is used by Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection (lines 110, 135, and 163), making the asynchronous replication unreliable or effectively skipped for normal completed requests. Detach cancellation (while preserving required context values/logging) before applying the timeout.

Independent replication goroutines can apply mutations out of order

Each successful write starts an independent goroutine with no per-resource ordering or serialization. For example, a successful unified Create followed immediately by Delete can run the legacy Delete first and the legacy Create second, leaving an object in legacy that no longer exists in unified storage. Consecutive updates can similarly overwrite newer legacy state with an older update. Since legacy APIs remain available as the stated safety measure, this produces persistent cross-store divergence; replication needs an ordered queue/keyed serialization or another ordering mechanism.

Legacy Update re-executes the original UpdatedObjectInfo instead of replaying the unified result

After Storage.Update has already evaluated objInfo against the unified object, the asynchronous legacy update receives the original objInfo and evaluates it again against legacy state. This regresses the prior implementation, which evaluated the update once and wrapped the resulting object for each store. UpdatedObjectInfo can represent a PATCH/apply operation and can depend on the old object, resource version, managed fields, or request-specific state; evaluating it again can yield a different object or fail due to the legacy object's version. As a result, successful unified updates may not be mirrored correctly to legacy. Capture and replay the object produced by the unified update (using an appropriate wrapper) rather than reusing objInfo.

Create storage failures are attributed to legacy metrics

When Storage.Create fails, the code calls `recordLegacyDuration` rather than `recordStorageDuration`. The analogous Update error path at line 129 has the same issue. Storage write failures in mode 3 will therefore be missing from storage error metrics and falsely inflate legacy errors, obscuring which backend failed.

Mode 3 tests do not verify asynchronous legacy replication

The tests return immediately after the unified operation and never wait for or assert the background legacy call. Moreover, both `legacyStoreMock` and `storageMock` share one testify Mock and define identical method expectations, so an expectation configured as a storage call can also satisfy the legacy call; there is no `AssertExpectations` call to establish that either occurred. Consequently these tests would pass if replication never runs (including when the caller context is canceled), and they do not detect the ordering or Update replay regressions. Use distinct backend mocks and synchronization (for example a channel/WaitGroup) to assert the legacy call and its arguments.

Feed and article content must be sanitized with the same trusted HTML policy used for normal posts before it is stored/rendered; the URL interpolated into the appended `imported_from` anchor must also be attribute-escaped.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same XSS concern in TopicEmbed.import: externally supplied contents are stored/rendered unsanitized, and the URL interpolated into the imported_from anchor must be escaped. It omits the separate nil-contents NoMethodError, but the core security issue matches.

false_positives.candidate:
Host validation does not protect the remote fetch after redirects

The only validation compares the initial URL host to `embeddable_host`, but `TopicEmbed.import_remote` follows that URL with `open(url)`. An allowed-host URL which redirects to an internal address (for example through an open redirect on the embedded site) causes the Discourse server to fetch the internal resource; its response can then be imported into a public topic. Validate every redirect target and resolved connection address against an allowlist, and reject private/link-local destinations.

Feed polling uses String#scrub despite the application's Ruby 1.9 compatibility

`String#scrub` was introduced in Ruby 2.1. This codebase still documents/supports Ruby 1.9-era execution, so enabling feed polling on those deployments raises `NoMethodError` on the first item and prevents all feed imports. Use a compatible encoding-cleanup implementation or explicitly raise the supported Ruby version before relying on `scrub`.

The new controller spec contradicts the asynchronous implementation

This example expects `TopicRetriever.new(...).retrieve` to be called during the request, but `EmbedController#best` now calls `Jobs.enqueue(:retrieve_topic, ...)` instead. The expectation is never satisfied, so the added spec suite fails. Update the test to assert the enqueue arguments (and retain separate job tests for retrieval), otherwise CI cannot pass and the intended asynchronous contract is untested.

The code sets X-Frame-Options: ALLOWALL which completely disables clickjacking protection. The referer validation can be bypassed (referer headers are easily spoofed), and the fallback to empty string for nil referer masks validation failures.
The ERB block closes with end if, which is invalid Ruby/ERB and will raise at render; it should just be end to close the if block.

Calling `i.content.scrub` assumes that `i.content` is always populated. However, many RSS feeds do not provide a `content` field, leading to a potential nil pointer exception when `i.content` is nil. A fallback to `description` should be implemented to prevent crashes.

An unescaped request header (request.referer) is interpolated into JavaScript without proper escaping, which can lead to XSS vulnerabilities if the referer contains malicious content. This issue can allow attackers to execute arbitrary scripts in the context of the application.

true_positives.golden_comment: Hardcoding maxSizeKB = 10 * 1024 ignores Discourse.SiteSettings['max_' + type + '_size_kb'], so the client-side limit can diverge from server-side and per-type settings (also applies to the 413 handler below).

Image conversion is invoked with the same input and output path

`OptimizedImage.downsize` is called with `tempfile.path` for both `from` and `to`. The generated `convert`/`gifsicle` command is therefore asked to overwrite its input while reading it; these tools can reject identical input/output files or truncate/corrupt the source depending on format/version. As a result, oversized uploads will commonly fail to be reduced (and may leave an invalid tempfile) before `Upload.create_for` runs. Write to a separate tempfile, verify conversion succeeded, then replace the original only after success.

The error shown for a server-side 413 always says 10 MB, even when the server/proxy rejected the upload because the site's configured image or attachment limit is different. This gives users an incorrect actionable limit and is inconsistent with the server configuration.

There are no tests for the new upload-time resize path, including successful reduction below `max_image_size_kb`, conversion failure handling, animated GIF handling, and preserving normal attachment limits. This is particularly important because the implementation mutates the uploaded tempfile before persistence and because the current same-path conversion call can fail silently before the upload validation response.

The action updates and saves the `TopicUser` record directly instead of using `TopicUser.change`, which is the normal notification-level update path. In particular, a topic-user row whose reason is still nil can subsequently satisfy `TopicUser.auto_track`'s `notifications_reason_id: nil` check and be automatically changed back to tracking, undoing a user's mute/unsubscribe choice. Use `TopicUser.change(current_user, topic_id, notification_level: ...)` so the change is marked with the `user_changed` reason and published consistently.

Typo in property name: 'stopNotificiationsText' should be 'stopNotificationsText' (missing 'n' in 'Notifications')

Use a portable temporary-file replacement or select the `sed -i` form based on the platform.

`end` is calculated from `slotStartTime` exactly as `start` is, so the condition only verifies that the slot starts before `workingHour.endTime`; it never verifies that the event ends before it. For round-robin events with a fixed host, a slot generated from a loose host's availability can therefore be retained even though the fixed host's shift ends partway through the event (for example, a 60-minute event starting at 09:30 with the fixed host available only until 10:00). The end value must include `eventLength` and be checked against the fixed host's availability.
true_positives.reasoning: The candidate identifies the same bug: end is derived from slotStartTime like start, so fixed-host working-hours validation only checks that the slot starts before workingHour.endTime and misses events that overrun the fixed host's shift. The suggested fix (include eventLength/end time) matches the golden comment.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using === for dayjs object comparison will always return false as it compares object references, not values. Use .isSame() method instead: dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, 'minutes').isSame(dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, minutes))
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Zero-length date overrides are never recognized as such

The code compares two newly-created Dayjs objects with `===`, which compares object identity and is always false even when `date.start` and `date.end` represent the same instant. Consequently, the special handling for a zero-length/full-day override never executes. Such an override can leave a slot at its boundary available instead of marking the host unavailable, allowing a booking during an intended day off. Compare the timestamps (for example with `isSame`) instead.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that === compares Dayjs object identity rather than timestamps, so equal start/end overrides are never detected, and both recommend isSame.

false_positives.candidate:
Multiple override windows on one day are treated as an intersection

The `find` callback returns `true` when a slot is outside any individual override window, and the outer code immediately rejects the slot. If a host has two availability override ranges on the same date, a slot inside the first range is necessarily outside the second range and is rejected. This makes all slots unavailable whenever date overrides contain multiple separate windows, rather than accepting slots covered by at least one window. The logic should first collect the overrides for the date and accept a slot if it fits within any applicable override range.

true_positives.golden_comment: Using retryCount: reminder.retryCount + 1 reads a possibly stale value and can lose increments under concurrency; consider an atomic increment via Prisma (increment: 1) to avoid race conditions (also applies to the similar update in the catch block).

The retry value is read in `findMany` and then written back as `reminder.retryCount + 1`. If two authorized cron invocations process the same unscheduled reminder concurrently, both can read (for example) 0 and both write 1 after failures. The row will then receive an extra retry despite two failed scheduling attempts, so the intended two-attempt limit is not enforced (and concurrent executions can continue submitting duplicate provider requests). Use an atomic database increment and/or atomically claim the reminder before scheduling; the catch-path update at line 195 has the same lost-update issue.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same lost-update race: retryCount is read and then written back as reminder.retryCount + 1, so concurrent executions can overwrite increments. Both also note the catch-path update has the same issue and recommend an atomic increment.

true_positives.golden_comment: The deletion logic in scheduleSMSReminders.ts incorrectly deletes non-SMS workflow reminders (e.g., Email, WhatsApp) that have retryCount > 1. This occurs because the retryCount condition within the OR clause for deletion lacks a method: WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, causing it to apply to all reminder types instead of only SMS reminders, which is the intended scope of this function.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
Retry cleanup is not restricted to SMS reminders

The new `retryCount > 1` branch is an OR condition without a `method: WorkflowMethods.SMS` constraint. Consequently, any non-SMS `WorkflowReminder` (for example, email or WhatsApp) whose retryCount exceeds one will be permanently deleted by this SMS cron endpoint, even though this job neither schedules nor owns those reminder types. Keep the retry threshold inside an SMS-scoped condition so this destructive cleanup cannot remove unrelated workflow reminder records.
true_positives.reasoning: Both describe the same deletion bug: the retryCount > 1 OR condition lacks a WorkflowMethods.SMS filter, causing non-SMS reminders to be deleted.

false_positives.candidate:
Reminders with no sendable message or recipient never consume retries

RetryCount is incremented only after `scheduleSMS` returns false or throws. When `message` is empty/null or `sendTo` is absent, the condition at this line is skipped entirely, leaving the reminder `scheduled: false` and `retryCount` unchanged. The cron will select and reprocess that permanently unsendable reminder on every run until its scheduled date, which preserves the retry loop this change is intended to stop. Mark these cases as failed attempts (or delete/cancel them explicitly) so they are bounded by the same retry policy.

This change deletes `findMany`, which previously applied authorization and filter conditions and returned records from `bookingTimeStatusDenormalized`. `getBaseConditions` only returns a SQL fragment; it does not accept or apply the caller's `findMany` arguments, perform the query, or provide an equivalent typed result API. Existing consumers of the exported `InsightsBookingService` that call `findMany` will fail to compile/runtime, and consumers migrated only to this method must reimplement query construction and risk omitting authorization conditions. Preserve `findMany` or introduce an equivalent supported raw-query method and migrate all callers atomically.

The team and org tests only compare `Prisma.Sql` objects constructed by the service with `Prisma.Sql` objects constructed in the expectation. They do not execute the predicates. The sole `$queryRaw` test at lines 481-484 uses user scope, which has neither the `ANY(${...})` array bindings nor the OR branches used by team/org authorization. Consequently, PostgreSQL serialization/type errors for array parameters, SQL precedence issues, or predicates that return unauthorized/missing bookings in the team and org scopes can pass this suite. Add database-backed tests for both scopes, including matching and non-matching team and member bookings.

false_negatives.golden_comment: In getBaseConditions(), the else if (filterConditions) and final else branches are unreachable. This is because getAuthorizationConditions() always returns a non-null Prisma.Sql object, making authConditions always truthy, which means only the first two if/else if conditions are ever evaluated.

Fetching userIdsFromOrg only when teamsFromOrg.length > 0 can exclude org-level members for orgs without child teams; consider deriving from teamIds (which includes orgId) or removing the guard so org-only orgs still include member user bookings.

true_positives.golden_comment: The Zod schema in parseRefreshTokenResponse uses computed property keys [z.string().toString()] and [z.string().optional().toString()] in minimumTokenResponseSchema, which is invalid Zod syntax and will throw a runtime error.
true_positives.matched_candidate:
The fallback token schema discards every expiry field from sync responses

Both computed property names evaluate to the same string (`"[object Object]"`), with the latter overwriting the former; they do not define a numeric-key catch-all. Moreover, `z.object` strips unknown keys by default. When credential syncing is enabled, a response such as `{ access_token, expiry_date }` is therefore parsed down to just `access_token` (plus the fabricated refresh token below). Callers then store an undefined/invalid expiry, causing tokens to be considered expired on every request; Zoom can persist `NaN` for `expiry_date`.

The candidate correctly explains both keys collapse to "[object Object]" and that z.object strips unknown keys, dropping expiry fields. Although the golden comment claims a runtime throw while the candidate describes silent data loss, they point to the same underlying bug.

true_positives.golden_comment: When APP_CREDENTIAL_SHARING_ENABLED and CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT are set, the refreshFunction helper returns the fetch Response, but several callers (for example GoogleCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting res.data, and HubspotCalendarService.refreshAccessToken expecting a HubspotToken) assume it returns the integration-specific token object. That mismatch will cause runtime errors in the sync-enabled path unless the return type or those call sites are adjusted.

Enabling `CALCOM_CREDENTIAL_SYNC_ENDPOINT` therefore makes refreshes for these integrations fail or save undefined token fields. The helper needs a normalized result contract (or all callers must explicitly parse the response consistently).
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the same bug: the sync-enabled refresh path returns a native fetch Response, while existing callers expect provider-specific token/data objects and access fields that do not exist on Response. The cited callers differ slightly, but the underlying contract mismatch and failure mode are identical.

true_positives.golden_comment: The `refreshOAuthTokens` function is passed `credentialId` instead of `userId`, which breaks the credential sync functionality by causing incorrect user lookups. This issue can lead to failures in syncing user credentials, impacting user experience.

`refreshOAuthTokens` expects its third argument to be a user ID and serializes it as `calcomUserId`, but this call passes `credentialId` rather than `credential.userId`. Credential primary keys are unrelated to user IDs, so the configured source application will refresh credentials for the wrong user or reject the request. If IDs happen to match another user, the returned token can be persisted onto this user's credential.
true_positives.reasoning: Both comments identify the same bug: refreshOAuthTokens is called with credentialId instead of the actual user ID (credential.userId), causing credential refresh/sync to target the wrong user or fail.

Salesforce service references Prisma without importing it

`prisma.credential.update` is called here, but this file has no `prisma` import. Type checking/building the app-store package will fail with `Cannot find name 'prisma'`, blocking the application build.

The outbound sync payload identifies this integration as `zoomvideo`, whereas the Zoom app/credential is consistently identified as `zoom` (for example, the OAuth callback creates `appId: "zoom"`). The handler performs `findFirst` and then separately creates a credential if none was found. Concurrent webhook deliveries for the same user and app can both observe no row and both create one. This invalidates the token, breaking subsequent token refreshes and causing authentication failures.

When the sync endpoint path is used, res is a fetch Response and has no .data; res?.data will be undefined and token.access_token will throw at runtime. This relies on a consistent return shape from refreshOAuthTokens, which isn’t guaranteed currently.

false_positives.candidate:
Cancellations can wait until after the reminder has been sent

Cancelled email reminders are only submitted to SendGrid when this 15-minute cron next runs and the reminder is within the next hour. For example, if a reminder is due in five minutes and the booking is cancelled immediately after a cron run, no cancellation request is made for up to 15 minutes, so SendGrid can deliver the reminder at its scheduled time. This leaves the primary cancelled-booking case unfixed for reminders cancelled shortly before they are due; cancellation needs to be performed promptly enough to beat the send time (or the scheduling job needs to run with a sufficiently tight guarantee).

The expired-reminder cleanup runs before the new cancellation loop and deletes every email reminder whose scheduledDate is at or before now, including rows marked cancelled. If the cron is late or SendGrid has not yet processed a send scheduled for that timestamp, the local record is removed and the later cancellation pass can no longer submit the required SendGrid cancellation. The scheduled email can consequently still be delivered, and there is no remaining row to retry cancellation. Cancelled reminders should be handled/cancelled before generic expiry cleanup, and failed cancellations should remain retryable.

This occurs during booking rescheduling/cancellation, and workflow/workflow step deletion/updates. Consequently, scheduled workflow reminders may not be reliably cancelled, potentially leaving them active.

This creates orphaned database entries and is inconsistent with the immediateDelete: false path, which marks the record as cancelled. The SendGrid DELETE API call is also omitted in this path.

The 'cancelled' field is nullable, which can lead to existing records having null values instead of a default of false. This can cause incorrect behavior in the application when checking the cancellation status of reminders.

Team admins and owners are incorrectly denied permission to add guests

A membership normally has one of these roles, so a team admin who is not the booking's assigned organizer (and an owner if the helpers are role-specific) fails this check even though the UI explicitly exposes this action to `isUserTeamAdminOrOwner`. Use `||` (or the project’s established combined-role authorization helper) so either privileged team role is accepted.

true_positives.golden_comment: The sendAddGuestsEmails function in email-manager.ts passes the full calendarEvent.attendees array when determining which attendees receive AttendeeScheduledEmail vs AttendeeAddGuestsEmail, but checks if newGuests.includes(attendee.email) where newGuests is the input guests array.

Existing addresses in a mixed request receive a new-booking email

The email sender is passed the original `guests` array rather than `uniqueGuests`. If a request contains one already-attending email plus one genuinely new email, `sendAddGuestsEmails` classifies the existing attendee as a newly added guest and sends it `AttendeeScheduledEmail` (a booking confirmation) even though no attendee was added for that address. Pass the filtered list of actually-created emails to ensure only new invitees receive the scheduled email.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify the same bug in sendAddGuestsEmails: the input guests array is used to classify attendees, so an existing attendee in a mixed request is treated as newly added and receives AttendeeScheduledEmail instead of the appropriate email.

true_positives.golden_comment: uniqueGuests filters out existing attendees and blacklisted emails but does not deduplicate duplicates within the input; createMany can insert duplicate attendee rows if the client submits repeated emails.

The API permits duplicate guest emails in a single request

`uniqueGuests` only filters out attendees that existed before this mutation; it never deduplicates `guests` itself. Although the dialog validates duplicates, callers can invoke the tRPC endpoint directly because the server schema has no uniqueness refinement. A request such as `["guest@example.com", "guest@example.com"]` therefore attempts to create duplicate attendee records (or fails the entire operation if a database uniqueness constraint exists), and can produce duplicate calendar/email effects. Deduplicate and normalize the input server-side, or reject duplicate input before `createMany`.
true_positives.reasoning: Both identify that uniqueGuests does not deduplicate repeated emails within the submitted guest list, allowing duplicate attendee creation.

false_positives.candidate:
Attendee-initiated updates use the attendee's calendar credentials instead of the organizer's

The handler explicitly authorizes any existing attendee at line 52, but obtains credentials from `ctx.user` here. For an attendee adding a guest, these are the attendee's integrations, not the booking organizer's destination-calendar credentials. `updateCalendarAttendees` will consequently be unable to update the organizer's calendar (or may target an inappropriate connected calendar), after the attendee rows have already been inserted. Resolve credentials for the booking owner/calendar connection when updating the booking's calendar.

A calendar-update failure leaves permanently inconsistent booking state

The new attendees are committed to the database at lines 92-106 before the external calendar update is attempted here. If `updateCalendarAttendees` throws, the mutation returns an error but the database still contains the guests; retrying then filters those emails as already present and rejects the request, so the caller cannot repair the missing calendar invitation/update through this feature. Add compensation/retry handling or structure the operation so failed external synchronization is recorded and can be retried rather than treating the database write as a completed update.

false_negatives.golden_comment: The addGuests.handler.ts blacklist check uses blacklistedGuestEmails.includes(guest) after lowercasing the blacklist but not the input guest emails, allowing attackers to bypass BLACKLISTED_GUEST_EMAILS restrictions by submitting emails with uppercase characters.

true_positives.matched_candidate:
Consume backup codes atomically

The backup code is read and validated from the initially fetched user record, then a separate unconditional update writes the modified array. Two credential requests using the same code can both read the unconsumed value before either update executes, both pass validation, and both receive sessions. This violates the stated exactly-once property and can let an attacker who races a legitimate user reuse a stolen code. Consume the code through a transaction/row lock or a conditional update that verifies the stored value has not changed, and reject the request when that update affects no rows.

true_positives.golden_comment: The code uses forEach with async callbacks, which causes asynchronous operations (e.g., calendar/video event deletions, payment refunds) to run concurrently without being awaited. This 'fire-and-forget' behavior leads to unhandled promise rejections, race conditions, and incomplete cleanup, as surrounding try-catch blocks cannot properly handle errors from these unawaited promises. Replace forEach with for...of loops or Promise.all() with map() to ensure proper sequential execution and error handling.
